bull.b: The much lower debt burden and rebuilt equity base give Tigo greater financial flexibility than in 2024. A cleaner balance sheet can support investment in growth markets, reduce interest pressure, and improve resilience if solar demand remains uneven over the next several quarters.

bull.t: Improved gross margin and cost discipline
bull.b: Higher gross margin and lower operating expenses indicate meaningful progress in the underlying operating model. If maintained beyond tariff-related benefits, this combination can improve earnings leverage, support competitiveness, and help Tigo reach profitability at a lower revenue scale.

Strong growth in Poland, Spain, and APAC shows that Tigo has regions with improving product demand beyond its weaker U.S. and selected European markets. Continued investment in successful geographies could broaden the revenue base and reduce dependence on any single market.

bear.t: Negative operating and free cash flow
bear.b: Negative operating and free cash flow create a gap between reported profitability and cash conversion. Sustained cash burn could require tighter working-capital management or external funding, limiting the resources available for product development and expansion until conversion improves.

The revenue decline and lower annual outlook indicate that recent profitability improvements are not yet supported by consistent top-line momentum. Continued volatility can reduce operating leverage, make planning more difficult, and keep margins vulnerable to weaker volume over the next several quarters.

bear.t: Exposure to subsidy and policy resets
bear.b: Tigo remains exposed to structural changes in solar support schemes and financing economics across several important markets. Reduced subsidies and longer homeowner payback periods can delay installations, pressure channel demand, and make recovery in the residential business gradual rather than immediate.
